STATUTORY COMPENSATION OF THE PERSONAL REPRESENTATIVE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Pat Morgan · Morgan Lee

PURPOSE OF THIS REFERENCE — STATUTORY COMPENSATION OF THE PERSONAL REPRESENTATIVE
This document describes, as general information, the statutory framework that California's Probate Code uses to set compensation for a personal representative — an executor named in a will or an administrator appointed without one — for ordinary services performed in administering the estate of Pat Morgan. Morgan Lee is identified here as the personal representative (or proposed personal representative) whose statutory compensation this reference describes. This document does not calculate, request, approve, or pay any specific dollar amount of compensation for Morgan Lee or for any other person, and it does not itself authorize any payment from Pat Morgan's estate. Under California law, a personal representative's compensation for ordinary services is ultimately allowed by the probate court as part of the estate administration, typically on a petition presented with an accounting; this document is background information for that process, not a substitute for it, and not a computation of what any specific estate's fee would be.

THE STATUTORY PERCENTAGE FEE SCHEDULE FOR THE PERSONAL REPRESENTATIVE'S ORDINARY SERVICES
Probate Code § 10800(a) sets a tiered statutory percentage schedule for a personal representative's compensation for ordinary services in administering an estate such as Pat Morgan's: four percent on the first $100,000 of the value of the estate accounted for; three percent on the next $100,000; two percent on the next $800,000; one percent on the next $9,000,000; one-half of one percent on the next $15,000,000; and, for all amounts above $25,000,000, a reasonable amount to be determined by the court. Section 10800(b) defines "the value of the estate accounted for by the personal representative," for purposes of this schedule, as the total amount of the appraisal value of property in the inventory, plus gains over the appraisal value on sales, plus receipts, less losses from the appraisal value on sales, without reference to encumbrances or other obligations on estate property — meaning the percentages are applied to that defined figure, not directly to the estate's gross fair market value or to its net value after debts.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) Subject to the provisions of this part, for ordinary services the personal representative shall receive compensation based on the value of the estate accounted for by the personal representative, as follows: (1) Four percent on the first one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000). (2) Three percent on the next one hundred thousand dollars ($100,000). (3) Two percent on the next eight hundred thousand dollars ($800,000). (4) One percent on the next nine million dollars ($9,000,000). (5) One-half of one percent on the next fifteen million dollars ($15,000,000). (6) For all amounts above twenty-five million dollars ($25,000,000), a reasonable amount to be determined by the court."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 10800(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 10800(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=10800.)
  "(b) For the purposes of this section, the value of the estate accounted for by the personal representative is the total amount of the appraisal value of property in the inventory, plus gains over the appraisal value on sales, plus receipts, less losses from the appraisal value on sales, without reference to encumbrances or other obligations on estate property."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 10800(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 10800(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=10800.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's statutory personal-representative compensation scheme — not a computation of any dollar amount for any specific decedent's estate or personal representative, and not a claim about which state's law governs any particular estate. This clause cites two subsections of the same statutory section, § 10800(a) and § 10800(b); they are not independent of one another. Honest gap: this clause does not address how the court treats jointly held, non-probate, or otherwise non-inventoried property for purposes of this percentage schedule, and it does not address the separate, similarly tiered statutory schedule for compensation of the attorney for the personal representative under Probate Code §§ 10810-10811, which this document does not cover.

EXTRAORDINARY SERVICES ARE COMPENSATED SEPARATELY, AT THE COURT'S DISCRETION — NOT BY A FIXED PERCENTAGE
Probate Code § 10801(a) allows the probate court, in addition to the ordinary-services compensation set by § 10800, to allow additional compensation to the personal representative for extraordinary services, in an amount the court determines is just and reasonable. Unlike the ordinary-services schedule, § 10801(a) does not itself specify a percentage, formula, or fixed rate for extraordinary-services compensation; the statute leaves that amount to the court's determination of what is just and reasonable in the circumstances.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) Subject to the provisions of this part, in addition to the compensation provided by Section 10800, the court may allow additional compensation for extraordinary services by the personal representative in an amount the court determines is just and reasonable."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 10801(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 10801(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=10801.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's statutory personal-representative compensation scheme — not a claim about whether any specific service performed in any particular decedent's estate would qualify as "extraordinary," and not an estimate of what amount a court would find just and reasonable. This clause cites a single statutory subsection, § 10801(a); no additional independent source was found for this. Honest gap: § 10801(a), on its own text, does not define "extraordinary services" or list examples of what qualifies; that determination is left to the court.

A WILL'S OWN COMPENSATION PROVISION DISPLACES THE STATUTORY SCHEDULE, AND NO SIDE AGREEMENT CAN PROVIDE MORE THAN THE STATUTE ALLOWS
Probate Code § 10802(a) provides that, except as otherwise provided in that section, if a decedent's will makes provision for the compensation of the personal representative, the compensation provided by the will — not the § 10800 statutory percentage schedule — is the full and only compensation for the personal representative's services. Section 10802(b) allows the personal representative to petition the court to be relieved from such a will provision, which the statute's later subsections tie to a noticed hearing and a court finding that relief is to the estate's advantage. Separately, Probate Code § 10803 provides that an agreement between the personal representative and an heir or devisee for compensation higher than that provided by this part is void — meaning that outside of a court-approved will provision or a court order, the personal representative and the estate's heirs or devisees cannot privately agree to pay more than the statutory or will-based amount.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) Except as otherwise provided in this section, if the decedent’s will makes provision for the compensation of the personal representative, the compensation provided by the will shall be the full and only compensation for the services of the personal representative."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 10802(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 10802(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=10802.)
  "(b) The personal representative may petition the court to be relieved from a provision of the will that provides for the compensation of the personal representative."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 10802(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 10802(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=10802.)
  "An agreement between the personal representative and an heir or devisee for higher compensation than that provided by this part is void."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 10803 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 10803 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=10803.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's statutory personal-representative compensation scheme — not a claim about whether any specific decedent's will contains a compensation provision, or about what any court would do with a petition for relief from one. This clause cites two separate, independently numbered statutory sections, § 10802(a)-(b) and § 10803; § 10802(a) and § 10802(b) are themselves subsections of the same section and are not independent of one another. Honest gap: this clause does not quote § 10802's remaining subsections, which set out the notice and best-interest-of-the-estate findings required before a court will relieve a personal representative from a will's compensation provision; it also does not address how § 10802 or § 10803 interact with a separate agreement for extraordinary-services compensation under § 10801.

A PERSONAL REPRESENTATIVE WHO IS ALSO AN ATTORNEY KEEPS THE PERSONAL REPRESENTATIVE'S OWN STATUTORY FEE
Probate Code § 10804 provides that, notwithstanding any provision in the decedent's will, a personal representative who is an attorney is entitled to receive the personal representative's own compensation as provided in this part, but is not entitled to also receive compensation for services as the attorney for the personal representative unless the court specifically approves that right to compensation in advance and finds that the arrangement is to the advantage, benefit, and best interests of the estate.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Notwithstanding any provision in the decedent’s will, a personal representative who is an attorney shall be entitled to receive the personal representative’s compensation as provided in this part, but shall not receive compensation for services as the attorney for the personal representative unless the court specifically approves the right to the compensation in advance and finds that the arrangement is to the advantage, benefit, and best interests of the decedent’s estate."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 10804 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 10804 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=10804.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's statutory personal-representative compensation scheme — not a claim about whether any specific personal representative is an attorney or about how any court would rule on an advance-approval request in any particular estate. This clause cites a single statutory section, § 10804; no additional independent source was found for this.

TWO OR MORE PERSONAL REPRESENTATIVES DIVIDE ONE STATUTORY FEE — EACH DOES NOT RECEIVE A FULL FEE
Probate Code § 10805 provides that if there are two or more personal representatives, the personal representative's compensation is apportioned among them by the court according to the services actually rendered by each, or as agreed to by the personal representatives. Under this section, the statutory percentage amount produced by the § 10800 schedule is a single amount to be divided among co-personal-representatives — not a separate full statutory fee for each of them.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "If there are two or more personal representatives, the personal representative’s compensation shall be apportioned among the personal representatives by the court according to the services actually rendered by each personal representative or as agreed to by the personal representatives."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 10805 (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 10805 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=10805.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's statutory personal-representative compensation scheme — not a claim about whether any specific decedent's estate has, or will have, more than one personal representative, or about how a court would apportion compensation among them. This clause cites a single statutory section, § 10805; no additional independent source was found for this.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT — STATUTORY COMPENSATION OF THE PERSONAL REPRESENTATIVE REFERENCE
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that I have reviewed the foregoing statutory compensation information in connection with the estate of Pat Morgan.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.
